stories.title: Seroprevalence and clinical correlates of fascioliasis among patients with hepatobiliary diseases in Urmia in Northwest Iran
stories.description: Fascioliasis is an important hepatobiliary zoonotic infection in which freshwater snails are intermediate hosts and livestock are the main definitive hosts. Humans become infected incidentally by ingesting metacercariae on aquatic plants or in contaminated water. Several regions of Iran are considered endemic for this infection; however, no comprehensive study of human fascioliasis has yet been conducted among hepatobiliary patients in the Urmia area. This study aimed to determine the seroprevalence of fascioliasis among patients with liver diseases referred to Imam Khomeini Hospital, Urmia, from 29 October 2024 to 26 February 2025. In this cross-sectional study, 313 sera were collected from patients with liver diseases referred to Imam Khomeini Hospital, Urmia. All sera were tested​ by anti-Fasciola hepatica IgG ELISA kit, and demographic, behavioral, and clinical data were recorded and analyzed using SPSS software. Geographic distribution of seropositive cases was mapped using geographic information system (GIS) mapping. Of the 313 patients examined, four (1.3%) tested seropositive for Fasciola infection; three of the four had a history of biliary stone and three resided in rural areas. Because of the small number of seropositive cases, the analysis was descriptive and no formal tests of association were performed. A live adult Fasciola sp. was endoscopically retrieved from the common bile duct of one seropositive-eosinophilic patient confirming active infection in this patient during the chronic biliary phase. The seroprevalence of fascioliasis among liver-disease patients in Urmia was low (1.3%), but numerically higher than the 0.33% recently reported in a different population survey in the same province. Given the parasite’s chronic course, its capacity to mimic other hepatobiliary disorders, clinicians should maintain caution for sporadic cases.

stories.title: Seroprevalence and associated risk factors of Trypanosoma evansi in camels in Fafan pastoral areas, eastern Ethiopia
stories.description: Camel trypanosomiasis, primarily caused by Trypanosoma evansi, is a major vector-borne disease that impairs camel productivity and pastoral livelihoods in arid and semi-arid regions. However, epidemiological evidence remains limited in camel-rearing areas of eastern Ethiopia. This study estimated T. evansi seroprevalence and identified associated factors among dromedary camels in selected districts of the Fafan Zone, Somali Regional State, Ethiopia. A cross-sectional study was conducted from July to December 2021 in the Goljano and Shabelley districts. Using multistage sampling, 570 camels were selected and tested for T. evansi antibodies using the Card Agglutination Test (CAT). Seroprevalence was estimated using descriptive statistics, and factors associated with seropositivity were identified through multivariable logistic regression following univariable screening (P < 0.25). Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05. Of the 570 camels examined, 145 were seropositive, giving an overall seroprevalence of 25.4% (95% CI: 21.9–29.2). Seroprevalence was 27.3% in Goljano District and 23.4% in Shabelley District. Poor body condition (AOR = 12.10; 95% CI: 7.62–19.49), absence of previous trypanocidal treatment (AOR = 4.89; 95% CI: 2.49–9.60), adult age (AOR = 2.63; 95% CI: 1.13–6.09), and old age (AOR = 2.68; 95% CI: 1.05–6.85), compared with young camels, were independently associated with T. evansi seropositivity. The findings indicate substantial exposure of camels to T. evansi in the study area. Strengthening surveillance, improving herd health management, promoting the rational use of trypanocidal drugs, and implementing integrated measures to reduce exposure to mechanical vectors may contribute to improved disease control.
